subject: Cooking
title: Brown Eggs vs. White: No Difference
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Brown Eggs vs. White: No Difference.

hook.text: Brown eggs cost more and seem more 'natural.' Inside the shell, they're identical to white eggs.

buildup.text: Egg color is determined by the breed of hen — nothing more. Brown hens lay brown eggs. White hens lay white.

discovery.text: Nutrition, taste, and cooking performance are identical regardless of shell color.

twist.text: Brown eggs cost more because brown hens are larger and eat more feed — the price reflects the hen, not the egg.

climax.text: What actually affects egg quality is the hen's diet and living conditions — not shell pigmentation.

punchline.text: You're paying extra for paint. The egg inside doesn't care.

quiz.question: Why do brown eggs typically cost more than white eggs?
options: Brown hens are larger and eat more feed

details.summary: Egg shell color is determined by the breed of hen, not diet, health, or nutritional content. Brown-feathered breeds lay brown eggs; white breeds lay white eggs. Nutritional content is identical when hens eat the same diet. Brown eggs cost more only because larger breeds eat more feed.
details.whyItMatters: The premium charged for brown eggs exploits the assumption that brown means natural or healthier. In reality, shell color is purely genetic and nutritionally irrelevant.
takeaways: Shell color is determined by hen breed genetics only
Nutritional content is identical given the same diet and conditions
Brown eggs cost more because the larger hens eat more feed

faq.question: Why do people assume brown eggs are healthier?
faq.answer: The association of brown with whole grain and natural products creates a health halo. Small farm eggs are often brown because heritage breeds tend to be brown-feathered. People conflate free-range farm freshness with shell color, but the two are independent variables.

faq.question: What actually determines egg nutritional quality?
faq.answer: The hen's diet is the primary factor. Hens fed omega-3 enriched feed produce eggs with more omega-3 fatty acids. Pasture-raised hens eating insects and plants produce eggs with more vitamins A and E. These factors matter; shell color does not.
